Part 2: Data and Analysis

In the midterm 1 folder there is a second folder called data. Inside the data folder, there is a .csv file called anolis_dat.csv. These data came from D. Luke Mahler, Liam J. Revell, Richard E. Glor, Jonathan B. Losos, ECOLOGICAL OPPORTUNITY AND THE RATE OF MORPHOLOGICAL EVOLUTION IN THE DIVERSIFICATION OF GREATER ANTILLEAN ANOLES, Evolution, Volume 64, Issue 9, 1 September 2010, Pages 2731–2745. The original research article is included in the data folder.

Anolis is a genus of lizards commonly known as anoles. Anoles are found throughout the Americas, but are especially diverse in the Caribbean. The data include morphological measurements for Anolis lizards from the islands of the Greater Antilles. These data can be used to study patterns of morphological evolution and adaptation in Anolis lizards.

The variables include:
- species: Species name of the anole lizard.
- habitat: Habitat type where the lizard was found.
- hindlimb_length_mm: Length of the lizard’s hindlimbs (in millimeters).
- tail_length_mm: Length of the lizard’s tail (in millimeters).
- body_length_mm: Length of the lizard’s body (in millimeters).
- toepad_lamellae_count: Count of lamellae on the lizard’s toepads.
- island: Island where the lizard was found.

Question 6. (2 points) Anole species were sampled from multiple islands. Which islands are represented in the data? Display the island names.

anolis %>% 
  distinct(island)
## # A tibble: 4 × 1
##   island     
##   <fct>      
## 1 Cuba       
## 2 Hispaniola 
## 3 Puerto Rico
## 4 Jamacia

Question 7. (4 points) Is sampling equal across islands? Create a plot to visualize the number of anole species sampled from each island. Be sure to label your axes and add a title.

anolis %>%
  select(island) %>% 
  ggplot(mapping=aes(x=island))+
  geom_bar(mapping=aes(fill=island))+
  labs(title="anole species sampled per island", y="# of unique species")

No, sampling is not equal across all islands. Cuba has the most sampling, followed by Hispaniola, while Puerto Rico and Jamaica have significantly less sampling.

Question 8. (2 points) Which habitat types are represented in the data? Display the names of the habitat types.

anolis %>%

##   <fct>       
## 1 Trunk-ground
## 2 Twig        
## 3 Grass-bush

Question 9. (4 points) Is sampling equal across habitat types? Create a plot to visualize the number of anole species sampled from each habitat type. Be sure to label your axes and add a title.

anolis %>% 
  select(habitat) %>% 
  ggplot(mapping=aes(x=habitat))+
  geom_bar(mapping=aes(fill=habitat))+
  labs(title="anole species sampled per habitat", y="# of unique species")

Sampling is not equal across habitat types. Trunk-ground was the most sampled habitat type, followed by Grass-bush. Trunk-crown was sampled the second least, and the least sampled habitat was Twig.

Question 10. (4 points) The morphology of anoles varies based on their habitat. How does the range of hindlimb length compare among different habitats? Create a plot to visualize the distribution of hindlimb lengths across habitat types. Be sure to label your axes and add a title.

anolis %>% 
  select(habitat, hindlimb_length_mm) %>% 
  ggplot(mapping=aes(x=habitat, y=hindlimb_length_mm))+
  geom_boxplot(mapping=aes(fill=habitat))+
  labs(title="hind limb length (mm) vs habitat")

Species in Trunk-ground habitats have the longest hindlimb length, followed by Trunk-crown, Grass-bush, and then finally Twig.

Question 11. (4 points) The plot above is compelling, but don’t we expect larger lizards to have longer limbs? What about tail length? Shouldn’t longer lizards have longer tails? To correct for this, make two new columns: 1. ratio_of_hindlimb_to_body, and 2. ratio_of_tail_to_body. Don’t forget to add these columns to the anolis data frame.

anolis <- anolis %>% 
  mutate(ratio_of_hindlimb_to_body=hindlimb_length_mm/body_length_mm,
         ratio_of_tail_to_body=tail_length_mm/body_length_mm)
anolis

Question 12. (4 points) Create a new plot that examines the distribution of ratio_of_hindlimb_to_body across habitat types. How does this plot differ from the one you made in Problem 10? Be sure to label your axes and add a title.

anolis %>% 
  select(habitat, ratio_of_hindlimb_to_body) %>% 
  ggplot(mapping=aes(x=habitat, y=ratio_of_hindlimb_to_body))+
  geom_boxplot(mapping=aes(fill=habitat))+
  labs(title="ratio of hindlimbs to body vs. habitat")

This plot instead shows length of limbs in comparison to body length.

This one indicates that species living in the Trunk-ground habitat type have the highest ratio of hindlimbs to body length, so similar to the first graph it can be said that they have longer limbseven when compared to body length. However, following that observation, the Grass-bush habitat has surpassed Trunk-crown quite significantly in this new graph, showing that the species living in Grass-bush have longer limbs compared to their body lengths than do species living in Trunk-crown habitats. Therefore in comparison to body length, species in Grass-bush have longer limbs than species in Trunk-crown.

Problem 13. (4 points) A longer tail provides better balance and agility. Create a plot that examines the relationship between body length and tail length. Color the points by habitat type and add a line of best fit. What does this plot suggest about the relationship between body length and tail length? What do you notice about lizards in the Grass-bush habitat? Be sure to label your axes and add a title.

anolis %>% 
  select(body_length_mm, tail_length_mm, habitat) %>% 
  ggplot(mapping=aes(x=body_length_mm, y=tail_length_mm))+
  geom_point(mapping=aes(color=habitat))+
  geom_smooth(method=lm, se=F)+
  labs(title="tail length (mm) vs. body length (mm)")
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

The body length of the species in the Twig habitat appears to have little to no relationship to tail length. The body lengths are about 40 mm while the tail lengths have a much wide range, from about 40 mm to about 65 mm. The line of best fit still indicates a positive relationship between body length and tail length however, tail length increasing with body length in order to increase balance and agility as the body gets larger.

Problem 14. (4 points) Toepad lamellae are transverse, plate-like structures found on the ventral surface of the digits. They are a key adaptation that allows anoles to cling to and move efficiently on smooth and vertical surfaces. What is the mean number of toepad lamellae for each habitat type?

anolis %>% 
  filter(habitat=="Grass-bush") %>% 
  summarise(grass_lamellae_mean=mean(toepad_lamellae_count))
## # A tibble: 1 × 1
##   grass_lamellae_mean
##                 <dbl>
## 1                28.3
anolis %>% 
  filter(habitat=="Trunk-crown") %>% 
  summarise(crown_lamellae_mean=mean(toepad_lamellae_count))
## # A tibble: 1 × 1
##   crown_lamellae_mean
##                 <dbl>
## 1                38.5
anolis %>% 
  filter(habitat=="Trunk-ground") %>% 
  summarise(ground_lamellae_mean=mean(toepad_lamellae_count))
## # A tibble: 1 × 1
##   ground_lamellae_mean
##                  <dbl>
## 1                 30.0
anolis %>% 
  filter(habitat=="Twig") %>% 
  summarise(twig_lamellae_mean=mean(toepad_lamellae_count))
## # A tibble: 1 × 1
##   twig_lamellae_mean
##                <dbl>
## 1               27.6

Problem 15. (5 points) The number of toepad lamellae is significantly different for trunk-crown species. But, is this consistent across all islands? Make a plot that shows the range in number of toepad lamellae by island for trunk-crown species only. Be sure to label your axes and add a title.

anolis %>% 
  select(toepad_lamellae_count, habitat, island) %>% 
  filter(habitat=="Trunk-crown") %>% 
  ggplot(mapping=aes(x=island, y=toepad_lamellae_count))+
  geom_boxplot(mapping=aes(fill=island))+
  labs(title="toepad lamellae vs. island for trunk-crown species")

It is not consistent across islands. Species that live in Trunk-crown habitat in Cuba have significantly higher numbers of toepad lamellae, followed by Hispaniola. Hispaniola’s lower quartile is within Jamaica’s upper quartile, but not by much. Finally, Puerto Rico has the lowest toepad lamellae count, approximately 10 below Cuba’s median.
